l: Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Hippolytus hears the Nurse's revelation, rejects her as a friend, and condemns women as a great evil. He keeps silent because of his oath, leaves the house while Theseus is away, and later appears before Theseus after Phædra's death.

l: Theseus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Theseus returns from the oracle and discovers that Phædra has hanged herself. After reading her letter accusing Hippolytus, he calls on Neptune to destroy his son and declares that Hippolytus will either die or be banished.

l: Nurse, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: The Nurse tries to cure Phædra's love by revealing it to Hippolytus, but Hippolytus angrily condemns her and Phædra blames her for destroying her. The Nurse admits that her attempt was unwise but says she acted from affection and a desire to find a remedy.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: The Chorus reflects on the destructive power of love and Venus, witnesses the exposure of Phædra's secret, and promises not to reveal it. It laments Phædra's death and warns Theseus to recall his curse against Hippolytus.

l: Venus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Venus is described as a destructive power whose influence brings calamity, including Phædra's love for Hippolytus. Phædra says that by dying she will gratify Venus, who has destroyed her.

l: Jove, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Jove is invoked in descriptions of Venus and Love, and Hippolytus questions why Jove allowed women to exist. Phædra calls Jove her ancestor and asks him to destroy the Nurse with fire.

l: Neptune, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Neptune is said to have promised Theseus three curses. Theseus invokes one of them against Hippolytus and expects Neptune either to send Hippolytus to the realm of Pluto or to drive him into exile.

l: Crete, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Phædra says that she will not disgrace the house of Crete by acting basely for the sake of her life.

l: Trœzene, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: The Chorus is identified as the noble daughters of Trœzene, whom Phædra asks to keep her secret.

l: women, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Hippolytus calls women a great evil, blames them for draining household wealth, and says that even a clever woman is dangerous. The Chorus instead laments the unhappy fate of women.

l: Eros, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Love is portrayed as a force that enters through the eyes, causes sweet affection, and brings calamity when directed destructively. Phædra's love for Hippolytus is called a disease that she can escape only through death.

l: marriage, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Marriage is associated with Venus, bridal chambers, dowries, household burdens, and Phædra's fear of dishonoring her family. The Chorus recalls Phædra's journey from Crete to Athens for her marriage to Theseus.

l: Phædra's illness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Phædra's disease is her forbidden love for Hippolytus. The Nurse attempts to find a remedy, but Phædra says the suffering is incurable and chooses death.

l: Phædra's suicide, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Phædra's suicide is carried out by hanging herself with a noose in her bridal chamber. Her death devastates Theseus and leaves his house in confusion and his children orphans.

l: letter (Phaedra's letter), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Phædra's letter is found sealed in her hand after her death. It accuses Hippolytus of forcing himself upon her and prompts Theseus to invoke Neptune's curse.

l: noose, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: The noose is the means by which Phædra kills herself. The servants find her suspended from it and call for a sword to cut the knot.

l: Phædra's accusation against Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Phædra's accusation appears in the letter she leaves for Theseus, claiming that Hippolytus approached her bed by force. Theseus believes the accusation and reacts by cursing his son.

l: Theseus's curse, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Theseus's curse calls on Neptune to destroy Hippolytus through one of the promised curses. Theseus says Hippolytus will either die or wander in exile, although the Chorus urges him to withdraw the prayer.

l: house (Phædra's household), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHORUS, PHÆDRA.
s: Theseus's house is thrown into confusion by Phædra's suicide, her accusation, and Theseus's curse. The Chorus fears that the house of its kings is ruined, while Theseus laments that it has been left desolate and that his children are orphans.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus denies Theseus's accusation that he defiled Theseus's wife and swears that he has remained sexually chaste. Theseus refuses to believe him, treats the letter left by the deceased woman as proof, and banishes Hippolytus from Athens and Troezen. After Theseus invokes his father, the ruler of the ocean, Hippolytus's horses are terrified by a bull from the sea, overturn the chariot, and drag Hippolytus to his death. The Messenger reports that Hippolytus was virtuous, while the Chorus reflects on the power of the Gods and Venus.

l: Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus denies having touched or desired Theseus's wife and swears by Zeus that he is innocent. He is banished by Theseus from Athens and the surrounding land, then suffers a fatal chariot accident after Theseus's curse is fulfilled.

l: Theseus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Theseus believes that Hippolytus has defiled his wife and refuses to accept Hippolytus's denial. He banishes Hippolytus and invokes his father, the ruler of the ocean, against him; after Hippolytus is injured, Theseus orders that he be brought before him.

l: Phaedra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Phaedra is identified as Theseus's deceased wife, whose letter accuses Hippolytus. Theseus treats her letter and death as decisive proof of Hippolytus's guilt.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus says that human happiness is uncertain and laments Hippolytus's exile. It later reflects on the calamity, praises Hippolytus's character indirectly through its grief, and describes the power of Venus over Gods and mortals.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Messenger reports that Hippolytus is dying after his chariot accident. He describes the sea-born bull, the terrified horses, the wrecked chariot, and Hippolytus's injuries, and declares that Hippolytus was virtuous.

l: the Gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Gods are invoked throughout the dispute as witnesses to oaths and as powers affecting human fortune. The Chorus says that their providence can lessen sorrow, while Theseus's appeal to the ruler of the ocean brings disaster upon Hippolytus.

l: Neptune, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Poseidon is referred to as Theseus's father and as the ruler of the ocean. Theseus invokes him to fulfill a curse against Hippolytus, and a destructive bull rises from the sea afterward.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Athens is the city from which Hippolytus is banished. Hippolytus bids farewell to the city before departing.

l: Trœzene, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Troezen is the land associated with Hippolytus's youth and hunting. Hippolytus bids farewell to its plain when he is forced into exile.

l: Hippolytus's exile, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus's exile is imposed by Theseus without an examination of the oath, proof, or seers' sayings. Hippolytus leaves his country in grief, and the Chorus mourns his departure.

l: Hippolytus's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus's death follows the fulfillment of Theseus's imprecation. He is dragged by the reins after the chariot overturns and is fatally injured against the rocks.

l: Theseus's curse, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Theseus asks the ruler of the ocean to destroy Hippolytus, and the curse is fulfilled through the sea-born bull and the horses' panic. Hippolytus recognizes the disaster as his father's imprecation while he is being dragged by the chariot.

l: Phædra's accusation against Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The accusation is that Hippolytus defiled Theseus's wife. Hippolytus rejects it as false, but Theseus accepts the deceased woman's letter as proof and banishes him.

l: chastity, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus claims that he is the most chaste man and that his body has remained undefiled by the couch of love. He says that he knows sexual acts only through report and pictures and has never desired Theseus's wife.

l: Hippolytus's chariot, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus's chariot carries him from the shore after he has been banished. A sea-born bull causes the horses to panic, and the chariot overturns, breaking its wheels and throwing Hippolytus into the reins.

l: Hippolytus's horses, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus's horses are harnessed when he prepares to leave the land. They become terrified by the bull from the sea, ignore Hippolytus's control, and drag the chariot into the rocks.

l: the bull from the sea, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The bull from the sea rises with a vast wave and a triple surge, bellowing fearfully. It follows the chariot's movements and drives the horses into panic until the chariot is destroyed.

l: letter (Phaedra's letter), The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, HIPPOLYTUS, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The letter left by the deceased woman accuses Hippolytus and is treated by Theseus as faithful proof that requires no interpretation by seers. Theseus relies on it instead of Hippolytus's oath and denial.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Diana reveals to Theseus that Phaedra falsely accused Hippolytus after falling in love with him, and that Theseus's curse caused his son's destruction. Hippolytus is brought in mortally injured, forgives Theseus, and dies after Diana promises him lasting honors at Troezene. Diana explains that Venus arranged the catastrophe because Hippolytus was chaste, while the Gods do not thwart one another's purposes. Theseus mourns his son, and the Chorus laments the disaster that has come upon the citizens.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Diana tells Theseus that he unjustly killed Hippolytus after believing Phaedra's false accusation. She explains the causes of the disaster, promises Hippolytus lasting honors at Troezene, and urges Hippolytus to forgive his father before she departs because it is not lawful for her to look upon the dying.

l: Theseus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Theseus learns that he was deceived by Phaedra and used one of the three wishes granted by his father against Hippolytus without waiting for proof. He bitterly repents, asks to die in his son's place, and mourns Hippolytus as Hippolytus forgives him before dying.

l: Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus is brought in severely mangled after his horses destroyed him, suffering intense pain from the injuries. He forgives Theseus at Diana's request, releases him from guilt for the killing, and dies while asking his father to cover his face.

l: Phaedra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Phaedra became enamored of Hippolytus and, fearing that her conduct would be examined, wrote a false letter accusing him. She dies before the truth can be fully established, but her death helps persuade Theseus of the accusation.

l: Venus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Venus is described as the deity most hateful to Diana and as having caused the catastrophe because she believed her honor had been offended by Hippolytus's chastity. Diana says that Venus destroyed Phaedra, Hippolytus, and Theseus, and vows to avenge herself on another mortal dear to Venus.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus sees Hippolytus approaching with his young flesh and head mangled and laments the double anguish inflicted on the house. After Hippolytus dies, it says that the citizens will shed many tears over the unexpected grief.

l: gods above, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Diana says that the Gods do not thwart one another's purposes but always give way to a deity who wills something. She also says that the Gods do not rejoice when the pious die, although they destroy the wicked with their children and houses.

l: Theseus's curse, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Theseus used one of the wishes granted by his father to curse Hippolytus, acting without examining proof or awaiting the voice of prophets. The curse brought about Hippolytus's destruction, and Theseus later recognizes that he was deceived.

l: Hippolytus's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus dies from the injuries inflicted when his horses destroyed him after Theseus's curse. Before dying, he forgives Theseus, and Diana promises that he will receive great honors and lasting remembrance among the virgins of Troezene.

l: Phædra's accusation against Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Phaedra's accusation is presented as false: she wrote a deceptive letter claiming wrongdoing by Hippolytus and persuaded Theseus to believe it. Theseus acted on the accusation without investigation, causing Hippolytus's death.

l: love, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Phaedra fell in love with Hippolytus after being affected by Venus, the deity hostile to those who delight in virginity. Her passion led to the false accusation that destroyed Hippolytus and contributed to the ruin of Theseus's household.

l: chastity, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, DIANA, THESEUS, CHORUS.
s: Hippolytus is shown to have remained chaste and to have reverenced the Gods, refusing Phaedra's advances and keeping the oaths imposed on him. Diana calls him pious and noble, and his chastity is identified as the reason Venus hated him.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes explain textual, grammatical, and interpretive difficulties in Euripides’ Hippolytus, often proposing alternative readings or emendations. They discuss Phaedra’s illness, shame, love, and assertions of chastity, including her struggle to name the man involved. They also clarify the account of Hippolytus’s chariot accident, including his horses, reins, clothing, and the bull from the sea. Theseus’s interpretation of Phaedra’s conduct and innocence is noted as involving a double meaning that he does not understand.

l: Hippolytus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes clarify details of Hippolytus’s chariot accident: he does not appear to change his dress, leans back while pulling the reins, and is compared to a sailor. The commentary also discusses proposed readings concerning his horse, clothing, and the sea-born bull that causes the disaster.

l: Phaedra, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Phaedra is described as struggling with shame and uncertainty before naming the man connected with her love. The notes discuss her illness, her assertions of chastity, and the double meaning in her claim that she had acted properly, a meaning Theseus does not understand.

l: Theseus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Theseus hears Phaedra’s assertion of chastity but is not intended to understand its double meaning. The notes present competing interpretations of how Phaedra’s words address her past conduct and her inability to persuade Theseus of her innocence.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Apollo explains that he saved Admetus from death by persuading the Fates to accept a substitute, and that Alcestis has agreed to die for her husband when neither of Admetus's parents would do so. Death comes to claim Alcestis, while Apollo predicts that Hercules will later take her away from Death. Alcestis prepares for death, says farewell to her children and husband, and asks Admetus not to remarry or bring a stepmother into the household. Admetus promises to remain faithful to her and mourns the life they will no longer share.

l: Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Apollo says that he served in Admetus's household after being punished by Jove and that he preserved the house because Admetus was pious. He obtained from the Fates an arrangement allowing Admetus to escape death if another person died in his place, and he predicts that Hercules will later take Alcestis from Death.

l: Death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Death comes to Admetus's palace to claim Alcestis, arguing with Apollo that she is the second person whose death he is owed. He says that he will perform the rites for Alcestis and consecrate her hair with his sword before taking her to the house of Pluto.

l: Chorus of Pherœans, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: The Chorus of Pherœans waits outside Admetus's palace and tries to learn whether Alcestis is alive or dead. It laments her coming death, praises her as the best of women, and fears that Admetus's life will no longer be worth living after her loss.

l: Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Alcestis gives her life so that Admetus may continue living, although she could have refused and married another man. Before dying, she prepares herself, visits the household altars, bids farewell to her bridal bed, and asks Admetus to care for their children and not take another wife.

l: Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Admetus survives because Alcestis agrees to die in his place, but he grieves as she approaches death. He promises that he will not remarry, will care for their children, and will remain faithful to Alcestis in life and after death.

l: Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Apollo predicts that Hercules, sent by Eurystheus to bring back a chariot and horses from Thrace, will be welcomed at Admetus's house and will take Alcestis away from Death by force.

l: the Fates, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: The Fates are persuaded by Apollo to allow Admetus to escape his impending death if another person dies in his place. Alcestis becomes the person who fulfills that condition.

l: Pluto, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Pluto is described as the ruler or occupant of the dark house of the dead. Alcestis imagines Pluto staring from beneath his black eyebrows as she is drawn toward the realm of the dead.

l: Admetus's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Admetus's palace is the place where Apollo served, Alcestis prepares for death, and Death arrives to claim her. Its silence and lack of ordinary funeral preparations initially leave the Chorus uncertain about Alcestis's condition.

l: Pluto's realm, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: The underworld is portrayed as the region beneath the earth where the dead dwell, associated with Pluto and the ferryman Charon. Alcestis believes she is being pulled toward its halls and gates.

l: substitution of Alcestis for Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Alcestis substitutes herself for Admetus by agreeing to die so that he may live. Neither Admetus's father nor his mother is willing to make the same sacrifice.

l: Alcestis's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Alcestis's death is destined for the present day, and she gradually loses her strength while bidding farewell to her husband, children, servants, and the light of the sun. Her death is presented as an act of devotion to Admetus and their children.

l: Admetus's escape from death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Admetus escapes the death that was approaching him because the Fates accept a substitute. His escape leaves Alcestis dying and causes him intense grief.

l: Admetus and Alcestis's marriage, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Alcestis says that she could have married another Thessalian and lived in royal comfort, but she chose to die for Admetus instead. She warns Admetus that a second marriage could bring a hostile stepmother to their children.

l: death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Death is treated as a power that cannot ordinarily be escaped, though Apollo temporarily alters its appointed course through a substitute. Alcestis and Admetus both recognize that mortality separates them, while Admetus imagines reunion after his own death.

l: bridal bed, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ALCESTIS.
s: Alcestis bids farewell to the bridal bed where she first joined Admetus and says that another woman may possess it after her death. Admetus promises to have an image of Alcestis placed on the bed so that he can embrace it and imagine holding her.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Alcestis dies after sacrificing herself for Admetus, entrusting their children to him and asking him not to remarry. Admetus mourns her, orders extensive funeral observances, and condemns his parents for refusing to die in his place. Hercules arrives while Alcestis is being mourned, and Admetus nevertheless receives him as a guest without revealing the full extent of his grief. The Chorus praises Alcestis's devotion and Admetus's hospitality, while the children lament their mother's death.

l: Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Alcestis dies for Admetus and entrusts their children to him, asking him not to marry another wife who might dishonor her. Before dying, she says farewell to her children and Admetus; the Chorus praises her as an exceptional and devoted wife.

l: Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Admetus promises Alcestis that he will not marry another wife and accepts responsibility for their children. He orders elaborate mourning and funeral observances, receives Hercules as a guest despite his grief, and angrily reproaches Pheres for refusing to die in his place.

l: children of Admetus and Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: The children are left motherless by Alcestis's death and lament that their household and lives have been orphaned. Admetus receives them from Alcestis and promises that he will not take another wife to rule over them.

l: Chorus of Pherœans, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: The Chorus consoles Admetus, saying that death is a debt all mortals must pay, and mourns Alcestis as an exceptional wife. It praises her sacrifice, condemns the failure of Admetus's parents to die for him, and praises Admetus's hospitality toward Hercules.

l: Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Hercules arrives seeking Admetus while undertaking a labor for Eurystheus: capturing the chariot-horses of Diomed, son of Mars. Admetus receives him as a guest despite the funeral, and Hercules does not initially know that Alcestis has died.

l: Pheres, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Pheres comes to Alcestis's funeral with adornments for her body and praises her for saving Admetus and preserving him from childlessness. Admetus rebukes Pheres for refusing to die for his son and rejects his attempt to honor Alcestis.

l: Pherae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Pherae is the city whose ruler is Admetus and whose people are ordered to share in mourning Alcestis. The city is to observe twelve months without the sound of pipes or the lyre.

l: Pluto's realm, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: The Chorus imagines Alcestis entering the sunless dwelling of Pluto and crossing the lake of Acheron. It asks Pluto and the ferryman of the dead to recognize that they are conveying an outstanding woman.

l: Alcestis's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Alcestis's death occurs because she accepts death in exchange for Admetus's life. Her death leaves Admetus, their children, and the household in profound grief, while the Chorus declares that it will be remembered in song.

l: Alcestis's funeral, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Admetus orders the corse to be carried out and commands mourning throughout Thessaly, including shorn locks, black clothing, and funeral honors. Pheres brings adornments, and Admetus's servants bear the body toward the tomb and pyre.

l: hospitality, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Admetus insists that Hercules must enter the house and be entertained even though Alcestis has died. He hides the full truth from Hercules, separates the guest chamber from the mourning household, and says that refusing a guest would make his house inhospitable.

l: self-sacrifice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. And I indeed with thee, as a friend with a friend, will bear this
s: Alcestis's self-sacrifice consists of dying so that Admetus may continue to live. The Chorus and Pheres treat this act as extraordinarily noble, while Admetus uses it to condemn Pheres and his mother for not sacrificing themselves for him.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Pheres and Admetus quarrel over Pheres's refusal to die for his son, and Pheres condemns Admetus for allowing Alcestis to die in his place. The servant of Admetus reproaches Hercules for feasting and singing while Alcestis is being mourned, then tells him that Alcestis has died. Hercules, shocked by the news and grateful for Admetus's hospitality, resolves to rescue Alcestis from Death and return her to the house of Admetus. The scene reflects on mortality, the uncertainty of life, and the obligations of hospitality.

l: Pheres, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Pheres argues that he was not bound by paternal or Grecian law to die for Admetus. He says that Admetus, unlike Alcestis, was unwilling to die, and he curses and disowns his son after their quarrel.

l: Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Admetus condemns Pheres for his lack of courage and for refusing to die for him. After Pheres blames him for Alcestis's death, Admetus orders him and his wife never to enter his house again.

l: Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Alcestis is praised as a noble and excellent woman who died for Admetus. The servant says that she was like a mother to the household and had saved the domestics from many troubles.

l: Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Hercules initially feasts and drinks in the house of Admetus without knowing that Alcestis has died. When the servant reveals the truth, Hercules resolves to seize Death or descend to the underworld and bring Alcestis back.

l: servant of Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: The servant resents Hercules for reveling while Alcestis is mourned, but explains that he had been ordered by Admetus to provide hospitality. He tells Hercules that Alcestis has died and directs him toward her tomb.

l: Admetus's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: The house of Admetus receives Hercules as a guest even while it is suffering the death of Alcestis. Its servants mourn Alcestis, while Admetus conceals the calamity from Hercules so that he will not be turned away.

l: Alcestis's funeral, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Alcestis's funeral procession proceeds toward a polished tomb beyond the suburbs on the road to Larissa. Admetus is occupied with carrying her body to burial when Hercules learns what has happened.

l: Alcestis's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Alcestis's death causes grief throughout the household and is used by Pheres as evidence of Admetus's cowardice. Hercules learns that she died in place of Admetus and decides to attempt her recovery.

l: Hercules's rescue of Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Hercules plans to ambush Death near Alcestis's tomb and force him to release her. If Death does not appear there, Hercules intends to descend to the underworld and ask its rulers to return Alcestis to Admetus.

l: Death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Death is described as the sable-vested king of the departed, whom Hercules intends to seize near Alcestis's tomb. Hercules believes that Death may be drinking libations there and plans to compel him to release Alcestis.

l: hospitality, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Admetus continues to offer Hercules hospitality despite the household's grief and Alcestis's death. Hercules regards this generosity as noble and resolves to repay Admetus by attempting to restore Alcestis.

l: death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. Desist, for the present calamity is sufficient; and do not, O son,
s: Hercules says that death is a debt all mortals must pay and that no one knows whether he will live until the next day. Pheres and Admetus's quarrel also contrasts the claims of old age, youth, self-preservation, and the sacrifice made by Alcestis.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus mourns Alcestis, who died in his place, and says that returning to his house and living without her is unbearable. The Chorus tells him to endure necessity and honor Alcestis, while Heracles arrives unaware of her death and later returns her after wrestling with Death at the tomb. Admetus initially refuses to accept the veiled woman Heracles brings, but recognizes her as Alcestis after taking her by the hand. Heracles says she must remain silent until the third day, and Admetus orders celebrations and sacrifices for the unexpected restoration of his happiness.

l: Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus grieves intensely for Alcestis and says that he would rather be dead than live without her. He fears entering his house, facing his children, enduring public reproach, and being accused of having allowed his wife to die in his place. He eventually accepts the woman brought by Heracles, recognizes her as Alcestis, and commands the citizens to celebrate.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus urges Admetus to enter the house and endure his grief, reminding him that many have lost wives and children. It declares that Necessity cannot be overcome by songs, medicines, sacrifices, or prayers, and advises that Alcestis's tomb be honored like a divine shrine.

l: Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Alcestis is described as Admetus's faithful and excellent wife, who died for him and left her love behind. Her likeness is recognized in the woman whom Heracles brings back, though she remains unable to speak until the appointed time has passed.

l: Death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Death has taken Alcestis from Admetus and deprived him of his wife. Heracles says that he seized Death by ambush and fought him at Alcestis's tomb in order to bring her back.

l: Admetus's palace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus's house has become a widowed and deserted place filled with reminders of Alcestis, including her empty bed, seat, and household floor. Admetus fears entering it because his children will mourn their mother there.

l: Admetus and Alcestis's marriage, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus recalls entering the palace with Alcestis amid Pelian torches, bridal songs, and revelry. Their marriage, once associated with happiness and noble birth, is now represented by groans, black clothing, and an empty couch.

l: Alcestis's death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Alcestis's death leaves Admetus convinced that his own life has become bitter and burdensome. He says that she has escaped future grief and toil, while he must continue living with the consequences of her loss.

l: substitution of Alcestis for Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Alcestis died in Admetus's place, allowing him to escape his own destined death. Admetus considers her sacrifice proof that she was the noblest of women and says that her tomb should be honored equally with the Gods.

l: Hercules's rescue of Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Heracles rescues Alcestis by confronting Death at the tomb and bringing her from beneath into the light. He gives her to Admetus but explains that she must remain silent until she is released from her consecrations to the Gods below and the third day has come.

l: mourning, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus's mourning includes groans, tears, despair, and a desire to die with Alcestis. He believes that time cannot heal him unless it is equivalent to death, though Heracles urges him not to grieve without limit.

l: widowhood, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus dreads widowhood because the empty house, his grieving children, and the sight of other women will continually remind him of Alcestis. He declares that no woman will lie with him and vows to remain faithful to his dead wife.

l: fate and necessity, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus presents Fate and Necessity as powers that cannot be resisted or cured by Orpheus's writings, medicines, sacrifices, or prayers. Admetus is told that weeping cannot bring the dead back from beneath, although the unexpected restoration of Alcestis ultimately changes the course of events.

l: hospitality, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus receives Heracles into his house despite his grief and conceals Alcestis's death so that Heracles will not be burdened with sorrow while visiting another host. Heracles criticizes him for this concealment but ultimately repays his hospitality by restoring Alcestis.

l: death and the afterlife, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, ADMETUS, CHORUS.
s: Admetus imagines the dead as happier than the living and longs for the houses of the dead and for Pluto's realm. The text also presents the dead as normally unable to return, but Heracles's struggle with Death allows Alcestis to come back, subject to ritual restrictions before she can speak.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: These notes explain passages and translation issues in Euripides’ Alcestis, especially Alcestis’ approaching death, funeral preparations, and return from Death. They discuss Death as the masculine figure corresponding to Θάνατος, who cuts Alcestis’ hair and consecrates her to the dead. They also describe Greek customs concerning corpses, mourning, burial, purification, tombs, and funeral rites. Several notes compare the play with other Greek and Latin authors, Shakespeare, and ancient inscriptions.

l: Alcestis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Alcestis is described as near death and as undergoing the preparations associated with a funeral. After Death cuts her hair and dedicates her to the dead, a contrary rite is understood to be necessary before she can again speak with and accompany Admetus.

l: Admetus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Admetus is the person whose companionship with Alcestis becomes possible again only after the ritual undoing of her dedication to the dead. The notes also connect his situation with the misfortune traditionally associated with surviving one’s children.

l: Death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Death is treated as the masculine personification corresponding to Θάνατος, for which Orcus was used as a Latin equivalent. Death cuts Alcestis’ hair and consecrates her to the dead, requiring a contrary ceremony before she can return to Admetus’ society.

l: Greek funeral customs, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Greek funeral customs included elaborate preparations for the dead, greater magnificence for those who died at an advanced age, and the display of a corpse with lustral water placed before the house. Mourners used ritual lamentations and farewells, cut or otherwise treated their hair, and observed purification after funerals; tombs were often magnificent structures near highways that could serve as landmarks or chapels.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Bacchus arrives in Thebes in mortal form to vindicate his mother Semele and establish his worship after Pentheus rejects him and persecutes the Bacchæ. Bacchus has driven the women of Cadmus's house, including Agave, Autonoe, and Ino, into Bacchic madness on the mountain and directs his Asian Chorus in sacred dances. Tiresias and Cadmus prepare to honor Bacchus, but Pentheus condemns the rites, orders the arrest of the stranger identified with Bacchus, and threatens punishment for his followers. Tiresias and Cadmus warn Pentheus that his impiety and resistance to the god will bring grief upon his house.

l: Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Bacchus, son of Jove and Semele, comes to Thebes in mortal form to vindicate his mother and make the city recognize him as a god. He has traveled through Lydia, Phrygia, Persia, Bactria, Media, Arabia, and Asia, establishing his mysteries, and he plans to set matters right in Thebes before moving elsewhere.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The Chorus consists of women from Asia who accompany Bacchus and celebrate him with dances, drums, hymns, and cries of Evoe. It praises the blessedness of those who understand the mysteries and live with holy purification.

l: Tiresias, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Tiresias comes dressed for Bacchic worship, wearing a deerskin, carrying a thyrsus, and crowned with ivy. He defends Bacchus, explains the benefits of wine and Bacchic excitement, urges Pentheus to honor the god, and warns that Pentheus is speaking and acting foolishly.

l: Cadmus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Cadmus comes prepared to honor Bacchus and agrees to dance with Tiresias despite his old age. He advises Pentheus to accept the god and warns him by recalling the fate of Actæon.

l: Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Pentheus, king of Thebes, rejects Bacchus and condemns the Bacchic rites as disorderly and corrupting. He orders the women who have joined the rites to be hunted or imprisoned, seeks the arrest of the stranger who claims to be Bacchus, and threatens to kill him.

l: Agave, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Agave, the daughter of Cadmus and mother of Pentheus, has been driven into Bacchic madness and is dwelling on the mountain with the other women of Cadmus's house.

l: Semele, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Semele, daughter of Cadmus and mother of Bacchus, is said to have borne Bacchus to Jove. She died when Jove's lightning struck her, and Bacchus comes to Thebes to defend her honor.

l: Jove, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Jove is identified as the father of Bacchus and the source of the lightning that killed Semele. The Chorus says that Jove later received the infant Bacchus and concealed him in his thigh until his birth was completed.

l: the Bacchæ, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The Bacchæ are the female followers of Bacchus who perform his dances and rites on the mountains. Bacchus says that he has brought Asian women as companions and that he will join the Bacchæ at Cithæron.

l: Mænads, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The Mænads are women driven into ecstatic Bacchic activity, wearing deerskins and carrying or being associated with the thyrsus. Bacchus identifies himself as their general and says that the women of Cadmus's house have joined them in the mountains.

l: Bacchants, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The Bacchants celebrate Bacchus through dancing, shouting, sacred music, and mountain rites. Their worship is described as involving purification, ivy crowns, deerskins, thyrsi, and the raw-eating sacrifice of goats.

l: Thebes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Thebes is the birthplace of Semele and the first Greek city in which Bacchus establishes his worship. Bacchus demands that Thebes recognize his divinity, while Pentheus attempts to suppress his rites there.

l: Cithaeron, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Cithæron is the mountain region where the Bacchæ and women of Cadmus's house are staying. Bacchus says that he will go there and share their dances.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Bacchus says that he has come to Greece after establishing his mysteries in foreign lands and that he first raises his Bacchic shout in Thebes. Tiresias says that Bacchus will become great throughout Greece.

l: the rites of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The Bacchic rites include dances, purification, the wearing of deerskins and ivy, the use of thyrsi and drums, and drinking wine. Pentheus condemns these rites and orders their participants to be arrested or driven from the mountains.

l: Bacchic madness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Bacchic madness has seized the women of Cadmus's house, driving them from the palace to the mountains. Tiresias says that Bacchic excitement and frenzy can bring prophetic insight, while Pentheus treats the condition as a dangerous disease.

l: Bacchic worship, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Bacchic worship is presented as honoring Bacchus through sacrifice, dancing, music, drinking, and initiation into his mysteries. Bacchus establishes this worship in Thebes, and Tiresias and Cadmus support it despite Pentheus's opposition.

l: Semele's death by lightning, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Semele's death by lightning is described as the result of Jove's thunderbolt striking her. Bacchus sees her tomb and the remains of her house, and he treats her death and the denial of his birth as insults that he must avenge.

l: Pentheus's persecution of the Bacchæ, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Pentheus's persecution of the Bacchæ includes imprisoning women in public strongholds, ordering the women absent from the city to be hunted, and seeking the arrest and execution of the stranger associated with Bacchus. His actions are opposed by Tiresias and Cadmus.

l: the thyrsus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The thyrsus is the ivy-clad staff carried by Bacchus, Tiresias, Cadmus, and the Bacchants in worship and dance. Pentheus orders it rejected, while the Chorus and Bacchæ treat it as a sacred emblem.

l: ivy, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Ivy is used to crown the heads of Bacchic worshipers and to adorn the thyrsus. Bacchus says he has covered Semele's tomb and the house with vine leaves, and Cadmus and Tiresias prepare to wear ivy in his honor.

l: wine, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: Wine is described as Bacchus's gift to mortals and as a drink that relieves grief, brings sleep, and causes forgetfulness of daily troubles. Tiresias says that wine should be honored in libations to the gods and enjoyed in Bacchic worship.

l: the palace of Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The palace of Pentheus is the place from which the women of Cadmus's house have been driven into Bacchic madness. Bacchus directs his Chorus to beat their drums around the palace so that Thebes may witness the rites.

l: the city of Thebes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE BACCHÆ.
s: The city of Thebes is required by Bacchus to recognize that it has not accepted his Bacchic rites. Pentheus seeks to suppress the worship in the city, while Tiresias and Cadmus urge its inhabitants to honor Bacchus.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Pentheus's servant brings the stranger to Pentheus, reporting that the stranger submitted calmly to arrest while the Bacchae escaped from prison when their chains and doors were miraculously released. Pentheus questions and threatens the stranger, orders him imprisoned, and plans to enslave or sell the Bacchae, while the stranger warns that Bacchus will punish him. Bacchus frees himself through divine power, causes Pentheus's palace to shake and fall into ruin, and returns to the Chorus. When Pentheus reappears, Bacchus tells him that the god who produces the vine delivered him and announces that a messenger from the mountain is coming.

l: Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Pentheus questions the stranger about his family, country, rites, appearance, and worship of Bacchus. He threatens to cut the stranger's hair, take his thyrsus, and imprison him, orders the Bacchae to be sold or enslaved, and later returns after the palace has been shaken and damaged, angry that the stranger escaped.

l: the servant, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The servant brings the captured stranger to Pentheus and reports that the stranger submitted calmly and even laughed while being bound. He also reports that the imprisoned Bacchae escaped when their fetters came loose and the prison doors opened without mortal hands.

l: Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Bacchus is identified as the son of Jove and Semele and as the god whose rites the stranger serves. He releases the stranger, shakes Pentheus's palace, kindles fire at Semele's tomb, and causes the house to fall into ruin.

l: the stranger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The stranger says that he comes from Lydia and that Bacchus persuaded him to bring the god's rites to Greece. Pentheus arrests and imprisons him, but he escapes through the intervention of Bacchus and returns to the Chorus, warning that Bacchus will pursue Pentheus.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The Chorus praises Bacchus, calls on him to restrain Pentheus, and celebrates when the stranger returns. It witnesses the shaking of Pentheus's palace and welcomes the stranger after his escape.

l: the Bacchae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The Bacchae whom Pentheus imprisoned escape when their fetters come loose and the prison doors open without mortal assistance. They dance in the meadows, invoke Bromius as their god, and are described as companions and worshippers of Bacchus.

l: Thebes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The stranger brings the rites of Bacchus to Thebes, and Pentheus treats the stranger's worship as an offense against the city. The Chorus describes Pentheus as an enemy of the gods and calls on Bacchus to act within Thebes.

l: the rites of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The rites are practiced by barbarians and are celebrated mostly at night, though some may be practiced by day. The stranger says that the rites are unlawful for the uninitiated to know and that they are worth knowing for those who sacrifice.

l: the palace of Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Bacchus causes Pentheus's palace to shake, and fire appears around the sacred tomb of Semele. Pentheus's servants labor unsuccessfully to extinguish the apparent fire, and the palace is then thrown down and shattered.

l: the prison, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: The prison holds the stranger after Pentheus orders him confined near the stable of horses. The Bacchae escape from the public prison when its doors open without mortal hands.

l: the chains and fetters, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Pentheus orders the stranger to be bound, but Bacchus prevents the chains from truly restraining him. The Bacchae's fetters are released from their feet without mortal assistance.

l: the destruction of Pentheus's house, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Bacchus shakes Pentheus's house and causes it to fall to the ground, with everything inside shattered. Pentheus mistakes the divine fire and destruction for an ordinary house fire and rushes about seeking water.

l: Pentheus's arrest of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Pentheus has the stranger, who is Bacchus, seized and bound after accusing him of insulting Pentheus and Thebes. He orders the stranger confined and threatens to punish him, but the arrest does not succeed.

l: Bacchus's escape, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, SERVANT. Pentheus, we are here; having caught this prey, for which you sent
s: Bacchus escapes from Pentheus's attempted imprisonment without difficulty. While Pentheus struggles with a bull and later attacks the air with a sword, Bacchus frees the stranger and brings him back to the Chorus.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: A messenger reports to Pentheus that the Bacchae on Cithaeron perform marvelous rites, summon water, milk, wine, and honey, and overpower men and cattle. Pentheus plans an armed assault on the Bacchae, but Bacchus persuades him to disguise himself as a woman and go secretly to observe them. Bacchus then leads the deluded Pentheus toward the mountain, while the Chorus celebrates Bacchus and anticipates Pentheus's punishment by the Maenads. The unit presents divine power, madness, and reverence toward the gods as forces that overcome Pentheus's resistance.

l: Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Pentheus rejects the messenger's report and orders an armed attack on the Bacchae. Bacchus persuades him to wear a woman's costume and travel secretly to Cithaeron, where Pentheus becomes confused and sees two suns, twin Thebes, and horns on Bacchus.

l: messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The messenger reports what he witnessed on Cithaeron: the Bacchae's rites, their miraculous sources of water and other substances, their destruction of cattle, and their victory over armed men. He urges Pentheus to receive Bacchus as a powerful god.

l: Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Bacchus warns Pentheus not to attack a god and offers to bring the Bacchae to him without arms. He disguises and guides Pentheus toward the mountain, intending that Pentheus be punished by his own mother.

l: the Bacchæ, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Bacchae sleep, awaken to Bacchic rites, and perform marvels with water, milk, wine, honey, fire, and serpents. They tear cattle apart, ravage nearby settlements, defeat armed men, and return to their springs to wash away the blood.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Chorus fears to speak openly to Pentheus but declares that Bacchus is inferior to none of the gods. It praises night-long dancing, reverence for divine law, and the eventual punishment of impious people, and it calls for the Bacchae to pursue Pentheus.

l: Agave, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Agave leads one of the three companies of Bacchae and awakens the women on the mountain. She helps drive away the men who ambush them and is expected to see Pentheus in hiding and attack him.

l: Thebes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Thebes is ruled by Pentheus, who seeks to protect it from the Bacchae. Pentheus is also concerned that the Bacchae's conduct will bring shame upon the city.

l: Cithaeron, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Cithaeron is the mountain where the Bacchae hold their revels. The messenger witnesses their rites and violence there, and Pentheus travels toward it in disguise.

l: wine, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Wine springs from the ground when a Bacchant places her wand upon it. The messenger says that wine ends grief and is associated with Venus and whatever is pleasant to mortals.

l: the thyrsus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The thyrsus produces miraculous effects when used by the Bacchae: one releases water from a rock, while another yields honey. Pentheus is instructed to carry a thyrsus as part of his woman's disguise.

l: Pentheus's woman's disguise, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Bacchus dresses Pentheus in a linen garment, a robe reaching his feet, a turban, a thyrsus, and a dappled deer-hide. He arranges Pentheus's hair and clothing so that he resembles a Bacchant or one of Cadmus's daughters.

l: the rites of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Bacchae perform Bacchic revelry by calling on Bacchus, dancing, wearing ivy and other garlands, and carrying thyrsi. Pentheus claims that he has practiced this revelry indoors, though Bacchus presents it as part of his transformation.

l: Bacchae's attack on the cattle, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Bacchae attack cattle with their bare hands, tearing apart calves and cows and scattering their remains. They also overpower bulls and later defeat armed men who attempt to resist them.

l: Pentheus's planned assault on the Bacchae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Pentheus orders the assembly of shield-bearers, riders, and archers so that he can attack the Bacchae. He abandons that plan when Bacchus offers to guide him secretly to observe them.

l: Pentheus's journey to Cithaeron, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Pentheus agrees to leave the city in disguise and follow Bacchus by deserted roads. Bacchus leads him toward Cithaeron, while Pentheus imagines that he can spy on and capture the Maenads.

l: divine punishment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Chorus says that the gods conceal the long reach of time and eventually pursue the impious. Bacchus declares that Pentheus will die after being led to the Bacchae and punished by his mother's hand.

l: Dionysian madness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: Bacchus intends to drive Pentheus out of his right mind so that he will willingly wear women's clothing. Pentheus then experiences distorted visions and behaves as though he has become a Bacchant.

l: divine power, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Bacchae's miraculous actions and victory over armed men demonstrate the power associated with Bacchus. The Chorus insists that divine strength is difficult to rouse but certain to chastise mortals who dishonor the gods.

l: wisdom and reverence toward the gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESSENGER. Pentheus, ruler o'er this Theban land, I come, having left
s: The Chorus identifies wisdom with respecting divine law and avoiding plans that exceed what is proper for mortals. It presents reverence toward the gods as the source of a life free from grief and condemns Pentheus's attempt to overcome a god by force.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Messenger reports that Pentheus was lured onto a pine on Cithaeron and torn apart by Agave, Ino, Autonoe, and the Mænads after Bacchus commanded their attack. Agave returns to Thebes carrying Pentheus's head, believing it to be the head of a lion, but Cadmus leads her to recognize what she has done. Bacchus declares that the family is being punished for rejecting his divinity and decrees exile for Cadmus and Agave, while Cadmus and Harmonia are destined to become dragons and rule over barbarians. The Chorus concludes that the gods bring about unexpected events.

l: Messenger, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Messenger reports Pentheus's death on Cithaeron and describes how the Mænads tore him apart. The Messenger then leaves to avoid meeting Agave before she returns to the palace.

l: the Bacchae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Chorus celebrates Bacchus's victory and initially rejoices over Pentheus's death. It later recognizes Agave's terrible deed, grieves for Cadmus, and concludes that divine events often occur unexpectedly.

l: Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Pentheus follows the stranger to Cithaeron and climbs a pine to watch the Mænads. After Bacchus commands the attack, Pentheus falls from the tree, pleads with Agave to spare him, and is killed and dismembered.

l: Agave, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Agave leads the attack on Pentheus and tears off his shoulder, later carrying his head to Thebes as though it were the head of a lion. Cadmus helps her recover her reason, and she recognizes that she has killed her son; Bacchus then decrees her exile.

l: Cadmus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Cadmus finds and brings back the scattered remains of Pentheus, then helps Agave understand that the head she carries is her son's. Bacchus condemns Cadmus to exile and foretells that Cadmus and Harmonia will become dragons and rule over barbarians.

l: Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Bacchus commands the Mænads to punish Pentheus and directs the events leading to his death. He declares that Cadmus's family is punished for insulting him and orders Cadmus and Agave into exile.

l: Mænads, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Mænads are seen on Cithaeron engaged in Bacchic revels. At Bacchus's command, they attack Pentheus, tear up the pine, and rip his body apart.

l: Thebes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Thebes is the city to which Agave returns with Pentheus's head and where Cadmus's house suffers its calamity. The Chorus declares allegiance to Bacchus rather than to Thebes.

l: Cithaeron, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Cithaeron is the mountain where the Mænads hold their revels and where Pentheus is killed. Agave later asks to be taken somewhere where she will neither see Cithaeron nor be reminded of the thyrsus.

l: Pentheus’s death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Pentheus's death occurs after the Mænads tear him from the pine and attack him under Bacchus's command. His body is scattered among the rocks and woods, while Agave carries his head on a thyrsus.

l: Pentheus’s dismemberment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Agave tears off one of Pentheus's shoulders, Ino tears the other side, and Autonoe and the other Mænads join in ripping him apart. His arms, feet, sides, and remaining flesh are separated and scattered.

l: the rites of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Bacchic revels take place among the Mænads on Cithaeron, who sing, dance, crown their thyrsi, and act under divine inspiration. Pentheus's attempt to observe and mock the revels leads to his destruction.

l: Agave's recognition of Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Cadmus asks Agave to look carefully at the head she carries and reminds her that Pentheus was her son. Agave then understands that the supposed lion's head is Pentheus's and realizes that she and her sisters killed him.

l: Cadmus's exile, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Bacchus decrees that Cadmus must leave his house and country as an aged exile. Cadmus laments that he will become a foreign sojourner, although he is also foretold to lead an army among barbarians.

l: divine punishment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: Bacchus presents Pentheus's death, the family's ruin, and the exile of Cadmus and Agave as punishment for insulting and refusing to honor him as a god. Cadmus acknowledges that the family recognized its error too late.

l: wisdom and reverence toward the gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, MESS. O house, which wast formerly prosperous in Greece! house of the
s: The Messenger states that wisdom and reverence for the gods are the most honorable and wisest course for mortals. Bacchus adds that Cadmus's family would have been happy if it had known how to be wise and accepted him as the son of Jupiter.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes explain passages, textual difficulties, and mythological parallels in the Bacchae, a play attributed to Euripides. They discuss Bacchanalian rites, including drums, cymbals, ivy, animal skins, dancing, and initiation, as well as Dionysus’s associations with prophecy, night, caves, and human sacrifice. The central catastrophe concerns Pentheus, whose madness and delusion lead to his death and dismemberment by Agave and the Mænads. The notes compare the story with accounts by Hyginus, Ovid, Oppian, Nonnus, and other ancient and later authors.

l: Bacchae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The Bacchae is examined through textual notes, proposed emendations, and comparisons with accounts by Hyginus, Ovid, Oppian, Nonnus, and other authors. Its subject matter includes Dionysian ritual, Pentheus’s madness, and Pentheus’s death and dismemberment.

l: Euripides, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Euripides is identified as the author whose Bacchae is being annotated. The notes sometimes defend or question the authenticity and interpretation of passages in the play, including claims that certain sections sound more like Proclus or may be interpolations.

l: Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Dionysus is associated with Bacchanalian rites, prophecy, initiation, caves, night, ivy, animal skins, and ecstatic cries. The notes also connect him with the epithet Ωμαδιος and with traditions of human sacrifice and the tearing apart of victims.

l: Pentheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Pentheus opposes Dionysian worship and is portrayed as over-cunning in religious matters. His madness produces delusions, including seeing double Thebes and mistaking Dionysian phenomena, before he becomes the victim of Agave and the Mænads.

l: Agave, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Agave is one of the women associated with the Bacchanalian rites and is described as boasting that she is undomestic. In the catastrophe, she participates in Pentheus’s destruction and treats his head as an ornament on the thyrsus before recognizing what has happened.

l: Mænads, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The Mænads perform ecstatic rites involving dancing, drums, cymbals, ivy, animal skins, and cries such as Evian. They tear Pentheus apart, and Oppian’s account cited in the notes says that they are transformed into panthers.

l: the rites of Bacchus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The Bacchanalian rites include music from drums and cymbals, dancing in caves, ivy and animal-skin adornments, thyrsi, ecstatic cries, and initiation. The notes associate these rites with Dionysus’s prophetic and supernatural powers.

l: Dionysian madness, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Dionysian madness causes delusion and distorted perception, as illustrated by Pentheus’s belief that he sees two Thebes and by his apparent transformation or perception as a bull. A passage from Nonnus cited in the notes describes Dionysus’s madness leaving Pentheus before he recognizes his fate.

l: Pentheus’s death, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Pentheus’s death is foreshadowed through obscure hints, dreams, and imagery of carrying or burial. The notes compare his fate with that of Actaeon and with accounts in Nonnus and Oppian.

l: Pentheus’s dismemberment, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Pentheus is torn apart by Agave and the Mænads in the catastrophe of the Bacchae. The notes connect this dismemberment with Dionysus’s epithet Ωμαδιος and cite traditions in which Pentheus is transformed into a bull before being destroyed.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Iolaus brings the sons of Hercules to the altars of the Gods in the land of Athens after Eurystheus has driven them from Argos and other parts of Greece. Copreus, herald of Eurystheus, tries to drag the suppliants away, but Demophoon protects them and refuses to surrender them. Iolaus appeals to Athenian kinship, Theseus's debt to Hercules, the protection owed to suppliants, and the honor of a free city. Copreus threatens to return with an Argive army, while Demophoon declares that Athens will not yield the Heraclids.

l: The Heraclidae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Heraclidae are represented as the persecuted family of Hercules, seeking refuge in the land of Athens. Their plight brings Demophoon into conflict with Eurystheus and the Argives.

l: Iolaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Iolaus, the aged companion and kinsman of Hercules, protects Hercules's children despite his own exile and insecurity. He brings them to the altars of the Gods, argues that Demophoon is bound to aid them by kinship and obligation, and praises Athens for defending them.

l: Copreus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Copreus, an Argive herald sent by Eurystheus, attempts to remove the Heraclids from the altar by force. After Demophoon prevents him, he threatens to return with a large Argive army and Eurystheus.

l: Demophoon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Demophoon, son of Theseus and ruler of the land, refuses to surrender the Heraclids. He cites the sanctity of the altar, his kinship with them, his debt to Hercules, and the disgrace of allowing suppliants to be seized by force.

l: Alcmena, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Alcmena, the mother of Hercules, is said to be preserving the female descendants within the temple while Iolaus leads the male children.

l: Eurystheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Eurystheus has driven the children of Hercules from their land and repeatedly sends heralds to demand their surrender. He is king of Mycenæ and intends to lead the Argive forces against Demophoon and the Heraclids.

l: Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Hercules is described as the father of the suppliants, the son of Jupiter and Alcmena, and a former companion of Iolaus. Theseus once aided Hercules by bringing him out of the underworld, creating an obligation that Iolaus invokes.

l: Theseus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Theseus, the father of Demophoon, is identified as a relative of Hercules's children through their shared descent from Pelops. He had also been aided by Hercules and Iolaus in the expedition for the belt, and Demophoon's duty to the Heraclids is partly based on that connection.

l: Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Chorus witnesses Copreus's violence against Iolaus and insists that the suppliants of the Gods must be protected. It urges Demophoon and Copreus to avoid violence and warns that the Argive army is approaching.

l: descendants of Hercules, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The sons of Hercules come as suppliants with Iolaus and sit at the altar after being driven from their homeland. Demophoon promises that they will not be dragged away, and Iolaus urges them to remember Athens as their dearest city if they regain their father's homes.

l: the Heraclids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Heraclids have been expelled from Argos and have sought protection at the altars in Athens. They are treated as related suppliants whom Demophoon must defend against Eurystheus.

l: Argives, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Argives are presented as the people from whom the Heraclids have been banished and whose laws condemn them to death. Copreus threatens that Argive forces will wage war against Athens if the Heraclids are not surrendered.

l: the Mycenaeans, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Mycenæans are associated with Eurystheus and his authority over the exiled Heraclids. Copreus claims that their opinion may oppose Athens's protection of the suppliants.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Athens is portrayed as a free city ruled by Demophoon and as a place where suppliants may seek protection at the Gods' altars. Its willingness to defend the Heraclids risks war with Argos but preserves its honor.

l: Marathon, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Marathon is the place where Iolaus and the Heraclids have arrived within the territory governed by Athens. They come there after wandering through Greece and seek refuge at the altars.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Argos is the Heraclids' former homeland and the place to which Eurystheus's herald demands that they be returned. Iolaus argues that, after their expulsion, they are no longer properly subject to Argos.

l: Mycenae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Mycenæ is ruled by Eurystheus, who claims authority to punish and recover the exiled Heraclids. Copreus says that allowing the Heraclids to be taken would enable Demophoon to gain Mycenæ as a friend.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Heraclids have been driven from every part of Greece and have wandered from one city to another. Iolaus appeals to the wider Greek reputation of Athens and says that Greece recognizes the former deeds of Hercules and Theseus.

l: the land of Erectheus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The land of Athens receives Iolaus and the Heraclids as suppliants. Demophoon declares that it is not subject to Argos and that its inhabitants may decide how to protect those who have taken refuge there.

l: the altars of the Gods, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The altars of the Gods provide the Heraclids with sanctuary after their exile. Copreus's attempt to remove them is treated as violence against both suppliants and the Gods.

l: the altar of Jupiter, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The altar of Jupiter is the immediate refuge where Iolaus and the Heraclids sit crowned as suppliants. Demophoon considers it disgraceful and impious to permit Copreus to violate this protection.

l: the Argive invasion, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The Argive invasion is threatened by Copreus after Demophoon refuses to surrender the Heraclids. Copreus claims that Eurystheus and a large force are waiting nearby, while Demophoon says that he does not fear Argos.

l: the persecution and exile of the Heraclids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: The persecution and exile of the Heraclids are carried out under Eurystheus's authority, forcing them from Argos and from other places where they attempt to settle. Iolaus remains with them because he would be ashamed to abandon the children after their father's death.

l: supplication, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Supplication is the means by which the Heraclids seek safety at the altars of the Gods. The Chorus and Demophoon treat the protection of suppliants as a religious and civic duty.

l: kinship and obligation, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Kinship and obligation bind Demophoon to the Heraclids through their descent from Pelops and through Theseus's former connection with Hercules. Iolaus also reminds Demophoon that Theseus was rescued from the underworld by Hercules.

l: honor and disgrace, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Honor and disgrace guide the decisions of both Iolaus and Demophoon. Iolaus refuses to abandon the children, while Demophoon says that allowing a foreigner to violate the altar would disgrace him and the city.

l: freedom and self-rule, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Freedom and self-rule are used to distinguish Athens from a city subject to Argive commands. Demophoon insists that he rules the land and will not allow Argos to dictate whether the Heraclids may remain.

l: Justice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THE HERACLIDÆ.
s: Justice is invoked by the Chorus, Iolaus, and Demophoon against the forced removal of the Heraclids. Iolaus argues that exiles from Argos are no longer properly subject to Argive authority, while Demophoon offers to hear any charge against them through a just process.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. This land is ever willing to aid in a just cause those in difficulty;
s: Demophon prepares Athens to receive the approaching Argive army, but reports that the oracle requires the sacrifice of a noble-born virgin to save the city and the Heraclids. Iolaus and the children of Hercules remain as suppliants, while Macaria freely offers herself for sacrifice so that her brothers and their protectors may live. A servant announces that Hyllus has arrived with an Athenian army, and Iolaus insists on joining the battle despite his age. The Argive and Athenian forces are about to engage under the opposing divine favor of Juno and Minerva.

l: Iolaus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. This land is ever willing to aid in a just cause those in difficulty;
s: Iolaus remains at the altar with the children as a suppliant and fears that Demophon's refusal to sacrifice a citizen's child will force them from Athens.
